column1: # clues.tsv for ft_convert_base — pedagogic hints only. NEVER state the expected value or the fix.
# Format: <hint><TAB><member CASE label><TAB>...   (fires if ANY member case fails)
# Lines are shown most-fundamental first; the first line doubles as the "foothold".

Before you touch the number, both bases have to earn the right to be used. What three things make a base unusable: too few symbols, a symbol that repeats, or a symbol reserved for sign? If either base fails any of those, what do you hand back?

Think of the job as two separate halves: first read nbr as a quantity using base_from, then write that quantity out using base_to. Are you keeping the reading rules and the writing rules apart, or mixing them? You have written both halves before in an earlier module — what did each of them have to handle?

Writing a number in a base means peeling off symbols by repeated division. A symbol's position in base_to is the digit it represents — so case matters, the symbol set is whatever the caller chose, and a negative value still needs its sign written first.
What does repeated division produce when the quantity is already nothing? Make sure that path still emits one symbol — which one, and where does base_to say to find it?
The most negative value cannot be flipped to its positive twin inside the same signed width. How will you read its symbols without ever holding that impossible positive in a too-small type?
